## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. The condition $T(x)=T(y)$ for all $T\in X^{*}$ implies that $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent (in fact, it implies $x=y$).

**Proof.** The hypothesis gives, for every $T\in X^{*}$,
$$
T(x)-T(y)=T(x-y)=0.
$$
Set $z:=x-y\in X$. We wish to show $z=0$.

We use the following standard corollary of the Hahn–Banach theorem:

> **Supporting functional corollary.** For every $z\in X$ with $z\neq 0$, there exists $T\in X^{*}$ with $\|T\|=1$ and $T(z)=\|z\|\neq 0$.

Indeed, define the linear functional $f$ on $\operatorname{span}\{z\}$ by $f(\alpha z)=\alpha\|z\|$. Then $\|f\|=1$ on this one-dimensional subspace, and by Hahn–Banach $f$ extends to some $T\in X^{*}$ with $\|T\|=1$, so $T(z)=\|z\|\neq 0$.

Now apply this to our $z=x-y$. If $z\neq 0$, the corollary furnishes a $T\in X^{*}$ with $T(z)=\|z\|\neq 0$, contradicting $T(z)=0$ (which holds for *all* $T\in X^{*}$ by hypothesis). Hence $z=0$, i.e.
$$
x=y.
$$

In particular $x=1\cdot y$, so $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent. (The degenerate case $x=y=0$ is also linearly dependent, since $0$ is linearly dependent with every vector.)

**Remark.** The conclusion is strictly stronger than linear dependence: the hypothesis forces $x=y$. Linear dependence alone ($x=\lambda y$ for some scalar $\lambda$) would not follow from a weaker condition; it is the full force of "for *all* $T\in X^{*}$" together with Hahn–Banach that pins down $x-y=0$ exactly. Note also that the argument uses only that $X$ is a normed space; completeness (the Banach property of $X$) is not actually required—only the completeness of $X^{*}$ is automatic, but the supporting-functional corollary holds for any normed space.

### PROOF COMPLETE
